items.title: Why address clustering matters more than balances
items.body: A single wallet's balance rarely tells the real story — most large holders spread funds across dozens of addresses to obscure size and intent. On-chain intelligence platforms use clustering heuristics (common-input-ownership, change-address detection, deposit-address fingerprinting) to link these addresses into one economic entity before flagging a 'whale.' That's why two wallets moving $60K each can be a single $120K whale move once clustered.

items.title: Exchange inflows and outflows as a sentiment signal
items.body: Large transfers INTO exchange wallets are often read as sell pressure (coins typically move to an exchange to be liquidated), while transfers OUT are read as accumulation or self-custody. It's a heuristic, not proof — OTC desks, custody rebalancing and cold-storage rotations all produce the same on-chain shape without any trading intent.

items.title: What actually happens when you 'swap' on a DEX
items.body: A decentralized exchange swap doesn't match a buyer to a seller directly — it trades against a liquidity pool using an automated market maker formula (like Uniswap's constant-product x*y=k). Your trade size relative to pool depth determines your price impact, which is why a $500K swap on a shallow pool can move price far more than the same swap on a deep one.

items.title: MEV: the tax you don't see on your transaction
items.body: Maximal extractable value (MEV) is profit block builders and searchers make by reordering, inserting, or censoring transactions within a block — commonly via sandwich attacks around large DEX swaps. It's a structural feature of public mempools, not a bug, and is one reason large trades are often routed through private order flow or MEV-protected RPCs.

items.title: Why mixers don't fully break traceability
items.body: Tools like coin mixers and privacy pools break the DIRECT link between deposit and withdrawal addresses, but they don't erase behavioral fingerprints — deposit/withdrawal timing correlation, amount matching, and address reuse elsewhere often let analysts probabilistically re-link funds. Full unlinkability requires far more discipline than most users apply in practice.

items.title: Stablecoins aren't all backed the same way
items.body: Fiat-collateralized stablecoins (like USDC, USDT) hold reserves off-chain in cash and short-term securities; crypto-collateralized ones (like DAI) are over-collateralized by on-chain assets to absorb price swings; algorithmic designs try to hold a peg through incentives alone with no hard collateral — the last category has the worst historical track record for depegging under stress.

items.title: The travel rule, in plain terms
items.body: FATF's 'travel rule' requires virtual asset service providers to pass along originator and beneficiary information (name, account number, sometimes address) on transfers above a jurisdiction's threshold — mirroring rules that have existed in traditional wire transfers for decades. It's the main reason exchange-to-exchange transfers increasingly carry more metadata than a wallet-to-wallet move.

items.title: What a 'wash trade' looks like on-chain
items.body: Wash trading — buying and selling the same asset to fake volume — leaves a distinct on-chain signature: near-identical amounts cycling between a small set of related addresses with little net position change. Volume alone is a weak signal; volume concentrated among a handful of clustered wallets is a much stronger tell.

items.title: Cold, hot, and warm wallets aren't just about temperature
items.body: Cold wallets (offline keys) hold the bulk of an exchange's reserves and move rarely; hot wallets sign automatically for user withdrawals and are deliberately kept thin to limit breach exposure; warm wallets sit in between, often multisig, used to top up hot wallets on a schedule. A sudden large cold-to-hot transfer is one of the more reliable pre-outflow signals analysts watch for.

items.title: Why 'total value locked' can mislead
items.body: TVL counts assets deposited into a protocol, but the same capital can be double- or triple-counted when it's re-deposited across composable protocols (e.g., a token that's staked, then the staking receipt is deposited elsewhere as collateral). Comparing raw TVL across protocols without accounting for this loop overstates real economic activity.

items.title: What makes a blockchain bridge a favorite exploit target
items.body: Bridges have to custody or mint assets based on messages from another chain, which means their security often reduces to a small multisig or a handful of validators — a much smaller attack surface than the base layers they connect. Historically, bridge hacks account for a disproportionate share of total DeFi losses relative to how much value they typically hold.

items.title: Proof of work vs proof of stake, the one-line version
items.body: Proof of work secures a chain by making block production expensive (computation, hardware, electricity); proof of stake secures it by making dishonest block production expensive (staked capital that gets slashed). Both aim for the same property — costly to attack — through different resources being put at risk.

items.title: Why 'burn' events aren't automatically bullish
items.body: Token burns permanently remove supply, which is often marketed as deflationary and price-positive, but the actual effect depends on whether the burned tokens were ever liquid, circulating supply in the first place. Burning tokens that were locked in a treasury and never sellable changes little about real market float.

items.title: The difference between custodial and non-custodial risk
items.body: Custodial wallets (exchanges, some apps) mean a third party holds your private keys — convenient, but you're exposed to their solvency and security. Non-custodial wallets mean you hold the keys yourself — you remove counterparty risk, but you also remove any safety net if a key is lost or a device is compromised.

items.title: Why NFT provenance is more useful than the image itself
items.body: An NFT's on-chain record — mint address, transaction history, prior holders — is often more valuable for authentication and forensics than the artwork it points to, since the image or metadata frequently lives off-chain and can be swapped or go offline. Analysts increasingly track NFTs the same way they track fungible tokens: by wallet history, not by picture.

items.title: Why a single large sell doesn't equal a market top
items.body: On-chain data can show a whale distributing a position, but it rarely shows WHY — tax-loss timing, fund redemptions, treasury diversification, and OTC settlement all create the same 'large sell' shape as a genuine bearish bet. Context (who, how it was routed, what followed) matters more than the transaction size alone.

items.title: What 'slashing' actually punishes in proof-of-stake
items.body: Slashing isn't a general performance penalty — it specifically targets provably dishonest or duplicated behavior (double-signing, equivocation) that could let a validator attack consensus. Simple downtime or being offline is typically punished separately and far more leniently than an actual safety violation.

items.title: Why exchange 'proof of reserves' isn't proof of solvency
items.body: A Merkle-tree proof of reserves can show an exchange holds certain assets at a point in time, but it says nothing about liabilities — what it owes customers. An exchange can hold real reserves and still be insolvent if what it owes exceeds what it holds; proof of reserves without proof of liabilities is half the picture.

items.title: The real reason gas fees spike
items.body: Gas prices spike from contention for limited block space, not from the network 'getting slower' — everyone bidding to get into the next block drives the auction price up. NFT mints, liquidations, and popular token launches are classic spike triggers because they concentrate demand into a narrow time window.

items.title: Why 'unrealized loss' whales aren't the same as insolvent whales
items.body: A wallet showing a large paper loss on a token position (cost basis versus current price) isn't in trouble unless it's leveraged or needs to close the position — plenty of large holders run multi-year theses through deep drawdowns without forced selling. Unrealized P&L is a data point, not a prediction of behavior.

items.title: How rug pulls usually show up in code before the chart
items.body: Many rug pulls are visible in the contract before the price ever moves: unlimited mint functions, an owner-only 'pause trading' switch, or liquidity that was never locked. Reading a token's contract permissions is a faster red-flag check than watching the chart for a crash that's already happened.

items.title: Why chain reorgs matter for exchange deposit confirmations
items.body: A blockchain reorg replaces the most recent blocks with a different version of history, which can un-confirm a transaction that briefly looked final — the reason exchanges require multiple confirmations before crediting a deposit. The required number scales with a chain's typical reorg depth and the value at stake.

items.title: What separates a fork from a fresh chain
items.body: A hard fork carries over a chain's full transaction history and existing balances up to the fork point, then diverges — holders of the original asset get the forked asset too. A brand-new chain (even one copying the same codebase) starts its ledger from zero, with no inherited balances at all.

items.title: Why compliance teams care about 'peel chains'
items.body: A peel chain is when a large balance moves through a long sequence of addresses, peeling off a small amount at each hop while the bulk continues onward — a common obfuscation pattern for both stolen funds and simple UTXO wallet behavior. Distinguishing genuine peel-chain laundering from ordinary wallet housekeeping is one of the harder calls in on-chain investigations.

items.title: Why 'circulating supply' is a judgment call, not a fact
items.body: Data providers differ on whether to exclude team/foundation tokens, locked vesting allocations, or known-lost coins from circulating supply — the same token can show meaningfully different market caps across trackers depending on those choices. Always check a provider's methodology before comparing market caps across assets.
